summary:
What was developed: Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a free browser app (laptop and phone, no login) that shows when the Sun and Earth are above the real local horizon at any Moon site and date. NASA LOLA terrain gives the true skyline in 720 directions, and JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions are tested against it every 3 hours.

How it addresses the challenge: A planner picks one of 19 preset sites (eight south-pole candidates, 11 past or planned landings) or any custom latitude and longitude. The app returns the percent of time with Sun, Earth and both, longest outages, solar power and a 0-100 score. It ranks all 19 sites for a date, finds the best start date, tests a relay satellite, lists dark periods, and computes the 18.6-year cycle. Results were checked against NASA illumination maps, Moon Trek and SPICE.

Why it is important: Launch dates slip, and the Sun and Earth sit low at the pole, so one ridge can cut power or contact for days. The project turns separate expert tools into one fast, plain-English comparison for planners, educators and the public.
details:
WHAT DOES THE PROJECT DO, AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers one planning question: for a chosen Moon site and date, when are the Sun and Earth above the real local horizon? At the south pole the Sun stays only a few degrees high, so one ridge can remove power or Earth contact for days.

The app reads NASA LOLA terrain (20 m at the pole), builds the true skyline in 720 directions, and tests JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions every 3 hours. It returns the percent of time with Sun, Earth and both, longest outages, time to sunset or Earthset, solar power, slope and a 0-100 mission score. Any of 19 preset sites or any latitude and longitude can be chosen. All 19 sites can be ranked for one date, the best start date can be found, a relay satellite tested, dark periods listed, and the full 18.6-year lunar cycle computed.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

Separate expert tools become one fast, side-by-side answer. Results are checked: Earth visibility is within 3.3 points of NASA's own illumination maps (10 sites), terrain height within 2.3 m of NASA Moon Trek (19 sites), and Sun and Earth directions agree with JPL Horizons and NASA SPICE. The far-side Chang'e-4 site correctly shows Earth at 0%. Uncertainty is shown as a range, and limits are stated: a planning aid, not landing clearance.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

When a launch slips, mission teams can re-plan in seconds instead of re-running several tools. Educators and the public can see why the south pole is hard, through a plain-English Learn tab and a shareable link for any result.

WHAT TOOLS HAVE BEEN USED?

- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python (SPICE check).

- Software: React 18, Vite, three.js, geotiff.js, SVG charts, Node.js test scripts (62 automated tests), Lighthouse.

- Data: NASA LOLA (PGDA 20 m polar, 118 m global), JPL Horizons (DE441), NASA PGDA illumination maps, NASA Moon Trek, NAIF SPICE.

- Hosting: Vercel (static site plus two small functions), GitHub (MIT licence).

- Hardware: none special. Everything runs in an ordinary browser, with no GPU, database or install.

HOW IS THE PROJECT CREATIVE?

Real terrain skylines and real Sun and Earth positions, normally in separate tools, are joined into one verdict. Visibility is shown as a whole-disc to any-part range instead of one falsely exact number. Dark periods get a plan: start, end, whether a stay fits, and the energy needed. An optional AI-written summary is rejected if it contains any number not in the results.

WHAT FACTORS WERE CONSIDERED?

- Energy: Sun height, panel output, dark periods, and energy to ride them out (load x hours).

- Accessibility: plain English, phone and laptop layouts, no login or install, keyboard labels, Lighthouse accessibility 100 on the checked screens.

- Cost: only free public data and open-source tools, an MIT-licensed code base, and an optional AI feature limited per visitor.
